paras: The Ku Klux Klan demonstration in Montgomery was a night visit to Montgomery, Alabama, by a group calling itself the Ku Klux Klan, reported by a Montgomery daily paper in 1919. No violence or victim was reported, but the account reached the Black press in June 1919 as evidence of a revived Klan meant to intimidate returning Black soldiers.

According to an unnamed Montgomery daily, the city "was visited last night by a Klu Klux Klan" that bore "all the ear marks" of the order that had "placed white supremacy back in the saddle" after what the paper called a "reign of terror" by "Negroes and sealawags." The quoted passage gives no date, size, route or act of force, and names no one. The article that quoted it added that the Klan had held other demonstrations at Birmingham, Mobile, Troy and smaller Alabama towns, and was reported riding by night in Texas, Oklahoma, Louisiana, Mississippi, Georgia, Florida and South Carolina.
No report of arrests or an official response to the visit appears in the coverage.

The visit reached the Black press third-hand, inside "The Blacks in Battle," an article from the periodical Jim Jam Jems that Cayton's Weekly of Seattle reprinted on 21 June 1919. The Jim Jam Jems writer admitted the magazine "has never been a defender of the black man" but argued that Black soldiers deserved a fair hearing. Introducing the Montgomery quotation with "Absorb some dusky facts," the article concluded that returning Black soldiers and officers "must be terrorized into servility and subservience" in the Klan's view.

In its editorial column the same issue of Cayton's Weekly explained that it reproduced the piece in full because its publisher, once among the harshest critics of Black people, now demanded "fair play for a greatly wronged people." No other Black-press report of the Montgomery visit was found.

accounts.label: Montgomery daily (as quoted)
accounts.gist: The city was visited 'last night' by a Klan resembling the old order that 'placed white supremacy back in the saddle'; the quoted passage describes no force.

accounts.label: Jim Jam Jems (reprinted by Cayton's Weekly)
accounts.gist: Places the Montgomery visit among Klan demonstrations across Alabama and seven other states and calls them an effort to terrorize returning Black soldiers.

framing.detail: Cayton's Weekly reprinted the Jim Jam Jems piece 'The Blacks in Battle' in full, introducing it with 'Absorb some dusky facts', and its editorial said the white man was 'sowing to the winds' by denying Black people a square deal.
